note: The VAmPI oracle: the polygon's known defects and the cells (account × endpoint × resource) that must produce a finding. The list is written by hand from VAmPI's access model (the polygon's README plus the `if vuln:` branches in its sources) and is NOT taken from barbican's output: a reference generated by the program under test tests it for consistency with itself. The rationale for the approach — ADR-0009. `expectedCells` is 27 on both variants, which is the same matrix in either mode: 3 accounts × (5 parameterless GET endpoints + users.read over 2 users + books.read over 2 books), the seven write endpoints and the excluded `db.createdb` being skipped before a request is built. Counted by hand and confirmed against `--dry-run`, which plans the matrix without sending anything and needs no Docker; not taken from a run against the polygon.
cellKey: account + endpoint + resource; resource = null on endpoints with no path parameters

user-directory-public.title: GET /users/v1 serves the list of all users with their email addresses to anybody, a request with no token included
user-directory-public.note: The policy declares the endpoint closed to everyone: a list of accounts with their email is not public data. The `vulnerable` mode does not affect it.

debug-endpoint-public.title: GET /users/v1/_debug serves all users together with their passwords and the admin flag, with no authentication
debug-endpoint-public.note: The status shows the bare fact of being public. What exactly leaks — passwords, not only names — is visible in the body alone, so the tool will not tell this finding from the previous one by severity. VAmPI does not fix it at vulnerable=0 either: this is "bad practice", not a switchable defect.

book-list-public.title: GET /books/v1 serves the list of all books with their owners' names without a token
book-list-public.note: There is exactly one finding — the anonymous one. For an authenticated user the list is meant by policy: by VAmPI's design it is his own shelf.

profile-any-user.title: GET /users/v1/{username} serves any user's profile to anyone who asks, the anonymous account included
profile-any-user.note: It requires substitution into a path template (ADR-0010): without a resource the endpoint is not probed. The `vulnerable` mode does not affect it — only the way the row is selected changes (in the vulnerable mode it is SQL concatenation), not the permission check, which is absent in both.

bola-book-secret.title: GET /books/v1/{book_title} in the vulnerable mode serves another user's book secret to any authenticated user
bola-book-secret.note: The only VAmPI defect distinguishable by response status between the modes: vulnerable=1 serves 200, vulnerable=0 filters the selection by owner and serves 404. Exactly the case ADR-0009 wrote about as "revisit once substitution into path templates arrives".

createdb-public.title: GET /createdb resets and recreates the database, and is available with no authentication
createdb-public.note: Formally it is visible in the status — 200 to the anonymous account where the policy declares a denial. But a request to it wipes the users and books created for the run, and the rest of the matrix is probed against an empty database. The endpoint is excluded by name; in the report it is listed as a skip with the reason `excluded`.

sqli-username.title: SQL injection in GET /users/v1/{username}: in the vulnerable mode the name is concatenated into the query text
sqli-username.note: The tool makes its requests with the declared resource identifiers and does not try payloads. The confirmation of an injection is in the response body.

mass-assignment-admin.title: POST /users/v1/register accepts an admin field and makes the registering user an administrator
mass-assignment-admin.note: An unsafe method plus confirmation in the body alone.

password-change-any.title: PUT /users/v1/{username}/password in the vulnerable mode changes the password of the user in the path rather than of the token's owner
password-change-any.note: The gravest defect of VAmPI and a wholly unreachable one: without --unsafe-methods the endpoint is not probed, and with it the tool still does not make up a request body.

email-update-bola.title: PUT /users/v1/{username}/email edits the email of the token's owner regardless of the name in the path, and in the vulnerable mode parses the address with a catastrophic regular expression on top of that
email-update-bola.note: The only cell where ADR-0009 measured a difference between the modes by status (204 against 400) — and it lies beyond the safe methods.

login-enumeration.title: POST /users/v1/login in the vulnerable mode answers differently to "no such user" and "wrong password"
login-enumeration.note: Both responses are 200. The difference is in the text of the message alone, that is, unreachable even with --unsafe-methods.

jwt-weak-key.title: The tokens are signed with the key "random": the signature is forged in seconds
jwt-weak-key.note: The tool tests access with the credentials it was given and does not forge them. This is a job for a separate check, not for the access matrix.

no-rate-limiting.title: There is no request rate limiting
no-rate-limiting.note: The tool throttles itself, and that is an invariant, not an option: it has no "no limits" mode. It therefore cannot detect the absence of someone else's limit by construction.
